claim: Monitoring autophagic flux is necessary for most autophagy studies.
source: Monitoring autophagic flux is necessary for most autophagy studies.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: The autophagic flux assays currently available for mammalian cells are generally complicated and do not yield highly quantitative results.
source: The autophagic flux assays currently available for mammalian cells are generally complicated and do not yield highly quantitative results.
evidence: This is a general assessment of existing methods based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Yeast autophagic flux is routinely monitored with the green fluorescence protein (GFP)-based processing assay.
source: Yeast autophagic flux is routinely monitored with the green fluorescence protein (GFP)-based processing assay, whereby the amount of GFP proteolytically released from GFP-containing reporters (e.g. GFP-Atg8), detected by immunoblotting, reflects autophagic flux.
evidence: This statement describes an established method in yeast autophagy research.

claim: The amount of GFP proteolytically released from GFP-containing reporters reflects autophagic flux in yeast.
source: Yeast autophagic flux is routinely monitored with the green fluorescence protein (GFP)-based processing assay, whereby the amount of GFP proteolytically released from GFP-containing reporters (e.g. GFP-Atg8), detected by immunoblotting, reflects autophagic flux.
evidence: This describes the principle of the established GFP-Atg8 processing assay in yeast.

claim: The GFP-based processing assay is typically inapplicable to mammalian cells because GFP is efficiently degraded in lysosomes.
source: However, this simple and effective assay is typically inapplicable to mammalian cells because GFP is efficiently degraded in lysosomes while the more proteolytically resistant red fluorescent protein (RFP) accumulates in lysosomes under basal conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and is further supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Red fluorescent protein (RFP) is more proteolytically resistant than GFP and accumulates in lysosomes under basal conditions.
source: However, this simple and effective assay is typically inapplicable to mammalian cells because GFP is efficiently degraded in lysosomes while the more proteolytically resistant red fluorescent protein (RFP) accumulates in lysosomes under basal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Halo is sensitive to lysosomal proteolysis but becomes resistant upon ligand binding.
source: We found that Halo is sensitive to lysosomal proteolysis but becomes resistant upon ligand binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pulse-labeled Halo-based reporters are proteolytically processed to generate Haloligand when delivered into lysosomes by autophagy.
source: When delivered into lysosomes by autophagy, pulse-labeled Halo-based reporters (e.g. Halo-LC3 and Halo-GFP) are proteolytically processed to generate Haloligand when delivered into lysosomes by autophagy.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 1, 3, and 4.

claim: The amount of free Haloligand detected by immunoblotting or in-gel fluorescence imaging reflects autophagic flux.
source: Hence, the amount of free Haloligand detected by immunoblotting or in-gel fluorescence imaging reflects autophagic flux.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Halo-based processing assay can monitor macroautophagy, selective autophagy, and bulk nonselective autophagy.
source: We demonstrate the applications of this assay by monitoring the autophagy pathways, macroautophagy, selective autophagy, and even bulk nonselective autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Autophagy is the lysosome-based degradation system in eukaryotes essential for cellular homeostasis.
source: Autophagy is the lysosome-based degradation system in eukaryotes essential for cellular homeostasis as part of intracellular quality control and intracellular remodeling during environmental adaptation (Bento et al., 2016; Kawabata and Yoshimori, 2020; Noda and Inagaki, 2015; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysregulated autophagy is associated with aging and diseases.
source: Dysregulated autophagy is associated with aging and diseases (Fleming et al., 2022; Kawabata and Yoshimori, 2020; Klionsky et al., 2021a; Mizushima and Levine, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Macroautophagy involves the formation of an autophagosome that sequesters material and fuses with lysosomes.
source: Macroautophagy and microautophagy are major autophagy pathways by which cytoplasmic material is delivered to lysosomes for degradation. The former pathway involves the formation of an autophagosome that sequesters material and fuses with lysosomes while the latter pathway occurs via direct invagination of the lysosomal membrane (Kawabata and Yoshimori, 2020; Noda and Inagaki, 2015; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microautophagy occurs via direct invagination of the lysosomal membrane.
source: Macroautophagy and microautophagy are major autophagy pathways by which cytoplasmic material is delivered to lysosomes for degradation. The former pathway involves the formation of an autophagosome that sequesters material and fuses with lysosomes while the latter pathway occurs via direct invagination of the lysosomal membrane (Kawabata and Yoshimori, 2020; Noda and Inagaki, 2015; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Autophagic flux refers to the amount of autophagic degradation.
source: Autophagic activity is the uninterrupted series of events that begins with material entering lysosomes and ends with their degradation by lysosomal hydrolases. The amount of autophagic degradation is often referred to as autophagic flux (Klionsky et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement defines a term and is supported by a citation.

claim: The GFP-Atg8 processing assay is the most commonly used quantitative assay for Saccharomyces cerevisiae autophagy.
source: Quantitative assays have been developed for Saccharomyces cerevisiae, with the GFP-Atg8 processing assay being the most commonly used (Shintani and Klionsky, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GFP-Atg8 localizes to both outer and inner autophagosomal membranes in yeast.
source: GFP-Atg8 localizes to both outer and inner autophagosomal membranes and is delivered into the vacuole as part of autophagic bodies (inner membrane-delimited vesicles), where GFP-Atg8 is then processed by vacuolar proteases.
evidence: This describes the established behavior of GFP-Atg8 in yeast.

claim: GFP is relatively stable against vacuolar proteolysis in yeast and accumulates in the vacuole as autophagy progresses.
source: Unlike Atg8, GFP is relatively stable against vacuolar proteolysis and accumulates in the vacuole as autophagy progresses.
evidence: This describes the established behavior of GFP in yeast vacuoles.

claim: The GFP-Atg8 processing assay can be adapted to monitor specific forms of autophagy by replacing Atg8 with a protein of interest.
source: Additionally, this assay can be adapted to monitor specific forms of autophagy by replacing Atg8 in the reporter with one's protein of interest, such as with the mitochondrial protein Om45 to monitor mitophagy (selective autophagy of mitochondria) (Kanki and Klionsky, 2008) or the cytosolic protein Pgk1 to monitor bulk nonselective autophagy (Welter et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature demonstrating these adaptations.

claim: GFP-Om45 can be used to monitor mitophagy in yeast.
source: Additionally, this assay can be adapted to monitor specific forms of autophagy by replacing Atg8 in the reporter with one's protein of interest, such as with the mitochondrial protein Om45 to monitor mitophagy (selective autophagy of mitochondria) (Kanki and Klionsky, 2008) or the cytosolic protein Pgk1 to monitor bulk nonselective autophagy (Welter et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GFP-Pgk1 can be used to monitor bulk nonselective autophagy in yeast.
source: Additionally, this assay can be adapted to monitor specific forms of autophagy by replacing Atg8 in the reporter with one's protein of interest, such as with the mitochondrial protein Om45 to monitor mitophagy (selective autophagy of mitochondria) (Kanki and Klionsky, 2008) or the cytosolic protein Pgk1 to monitor bulk nonselective autophagy (Welter et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GFP is rapidly degraded in mammalian lysosomes.
source: Implementing the GFP-Atg8 processing assay in mammalian cells (using LC3 and GABARAP family proteins) has been challenging because GFP is rapidly degraded in mammalian lysosomes (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Only a few studies have succeeded in detecting the release of free GFP from GFP-LC3 in mammalian cells.
source: Only a few studies have succeeded in detecting the release of free GFP (Gao et al., 2008; Hosokawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The success rate of detecting free GFP from GFP-LC3 could be increased by raising the luminal pH of lysosomes with nonsaturating concentrations of lysosomotropic agents.
source: Although the success rate could be increased by raising the luminal pH of lysosomes with nonsaturating concentrations of lysosomotropic agents (Gao et al., 2008; Klionsky et al., 2021b), doing so might also affect GFP-LC3 processing itself and thus would require careful optimization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Raising lysosomal pH with lysosomotropic agents might affect GFP-LC3 processing itself.
source: Although the success rate could be increased by raising the luminal pH of lysosomes with nonsaturating concentrations of lysosomotropic agents (Gao et al., 2008; Klionsky et al., 2021b), doing so might also affect GFP-LC3 processing itself and thus would require careful optimization.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential side effects of the method.

claim: In mammalian cells, autophagic flux is often estimated from the amount of selective autophagic cargo degraded.
source: In mammalian cells, autophagic flux is often estimated from the amount of selective autophagic cargo degraded or, with the LC3 turnover assay, the amount of LC3-II produced in the presence of a lysosomal inhibitor (i.e. the amount of LC3-II that would have otherwise been degraded; Klionsky et al., 2021b; Mizushima and Murphy, 2020; Mizushima and Yoshimori, 2007).
evidence: This statement describes established methods and is supported by citations.

claim: The LC3 turnover assay estimates autophagic flux from the amount of LC3-II produced in the presence of a lysosomal inhibitor.
source: In mammalian cells, autophagic flux is often estimated from the amount of selective autophagic cargo degraded or, with the LC3 turnover assay, the amount of LC3-II produced in the presence of a lysosomal inhibitor (i.e. the amount of LC3-II that would have otherwise been degraded; Klionsky et al., 2021b; Mizushima and Murphy, 2020; Mizushima and Yoshimori, 2007).
evidence: This statement describes an established method and is supported by citations.

claim: RFP-GFP-LC3 can be used to monitor autophagic flux based on the reduction in GFP fluorescence compared to the relatively unchanging fluorescence of the lysosome-resistant RFP.
source: Autophagic flux can also be monitored with the fluorescent reporters, RFP-GFP-LC3 (Kimura et al., 2007) and GFP-LC3-RFP (Kaizuka et al., 2016), with which autophagic flux is determined from the reduction in GFP fluorescence compared to the relatively unchanging fluorescence of the lysosome-resistant RFP and cytosol-localizing RFP, respectively.
evidence: This statement describes an established method and is supported by citations.

claim: GFP-LC3-RFP can be used to monitor autophagic flux based on the reduction in GFP fluorescence compared to cytosol-localizing RFP.
source: Autophagic flux can also be monitored with the fluorescent reporters, RFP-GFP-LC3 (Kimura et al., 2007) and GFP-LC3-RFP (Kaizuka et al., 2016), with which autophagic flux is determined from the reduction in GFP fluorescence compared to the relatively unchanging fluorescence of the lysosome-resistant RFP and cytosol-localizing RFP, respectively.
evidence: This statement describes an established method and is supported by citations.

claim: Some autophagic flux assays require the use of a lysosomal inhibitor control, which can limit the assay's dynamic range.
source: Some require the use of a lysosomal inhibitor control, which can limit the assay's dynamic range (Liebl et al., 2022) and cause side-effects (Florey et al., 2015; Juhász, 2012), while others are complicated or are low in sensitivity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lysosomal inhibitor controls can cause side-effects.
source: Some require the use of a lysosomal inhibitor control, which can limit the assay's dynamic range (Liebl et al., 2022) and cause side-effects (Florey et al., 2015; Juhász, 2012), while others are complicated or are low in sensitivity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A small amount of free mGFP was produced from mGFP-LC3B in wild-type HeLa cells but not in FIP200 knockout cells under both growing and starvation conditions.
source: With monomeric GFP (mGFP)-LC3B, a small amount of free mGFP was produced in wild-type HeLa cells but not in FIP200 knockout (KO) cells under both growing and starvation conditions, indicating that free mGFP was generated in an autophagy-dependent manner (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Free mGFP from mGFP-LC3B is generated in an autophagy-dependent manner.
source: With monomeric GFP (mGFP)-LC3B, a small amount of free mGFP was produced in wild-type HeLa cells but not in FIP200 knockout (KO) cells under both growing and starvation conditions, indicating that free mGFP was generated in an autophagy-dependent manner (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that free mGFP is not produced in FIP200 KO cells, which lack autophagy.

claim: A starvation-induced decrease of mGFP-LC3B levels was detected, but an increase in free mGFP levels was not.
source: However, although a starvation-induced decrease of mGFP-LC3B levels was detected, an increase in free mGFP levels was not (Figure 1a, left) as mGFP is degraded in mammalian lysosomes like other GFPs (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1a and a citation to prior literature.

claim: mGFP is degraded in mammalian lysosomes like other GFPs.
source: However, although a starvation-induced decrease of mGFP-LC3B levels was detected, an increase in free mGFP levels was not (Figure 1a, left) as mGFP is degraded in mammalian lysosomes like other GFPs (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Replacing mGFP with mRFP in the LC3 reporter allowed for an increase in free mRFP levels upon starvation to be detected.
source: Replacing mGFP with the proteolytically resistant monomeric RFP (mRFP) (Katayama et al., 2008) allowed for an increase in free mRFP levels upon starvation to be detected (Figure 1a, right), but the increase was not apparent due to the pre-existing mRFP band (Figure 1a, right) that probably resulted from basal autophagy-mediated lysosomal accumulation (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1a and citations to prior literature.

claim: The increase in free mRFP upon starvation was not apparent due to a pre-existing mRFP band that probably resulted from basal autophagy-mediated lysosomal accumulation.
source: Replacing mGFP with the proteolytically resistant monomeric RFP (mRFP) (Katayama et al., 2008) allowed for an increase in free mRFP levels upon starvation to be detected (Figure 1a, right), but the increase was not apparent due to the pre-existing mRFP band (Figure 1a, right) that probably resulted from basal autophagy-mediated lysosomal accumulation (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1a, a citation to prior literature, and inference about the cause.

claim: It is difficult to detect mammalian autophagic flux with a GFP- or RFP-tagged LC3 processing assay.
source: Hence, it is difficult to detect mammalian autophagic flux with a GFP- or RFP-tagged LC3 processing assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data with mGFP-LC3B and mRFP-LC3B.

claim: After 6 hr of starvation, a starvation-induced decrease in labeled and unlabeled Halo-LC3B was observed.
source: After 6 hr of starvation, a starvation-induced decrease in labeled and unlabeled Halo-LC3B was observed by immunoblotting and, for labeled HaloTMR-LC3B, in-gel fluorescence detection (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Free Halo was detected only for HaloTMR-LC3B (ligand-bound) and not for unlabeled Halo-LC3B.
source: Strikingly, free Halo was detected only for HaloTMR-LC3B.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The decrease in Halo-LC3B and HaloTMR-LC3B levels and appearance of free HaloTMR were dependent on autophagy.
source: The decrease in Halo-LC3B and HaloTMR-LC3B levels and appearance of free HaloTMR were dependent on autophagy and lysosomal enzymatic activity as they were suppressed in FIP200 KO cells (Figure 1b–c) and by the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (Klionsky et al., 2008; Mauvezin et al., 2015; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1b-c showing suppression in FIP200 KO cells and with bafilomycin A1.

claim: The decrease in Halo-LC3B and HaloTMR-LC3B levels and appearance of free HaloTMR were dependent on lysosomal enzymatic activity.
source: The decrease in Halo-LC3B and HaloTMR-LC3B levels and appearance of free HaloTMR were dependent on autophagy and lysosomal enzymatic activity as they were suppressed in FIP200 KO cells (Figure 1b–c) and by the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (Klionsky et al., 2008; Mauvezin et al., 2015; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1c showing suppression with bafilomycin A1 and citations to prior literature.

claim: Removal of the ligand was enough to prevent further labeling of Halo-LC3B.
source: Removal of the ligand was enough to prevent further labeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, compare lanes 8–10), avoiding the need for a blocking agent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The generation of free SNAP was not detected from ligand-free and ligand-bound SNAP-LC3 during starvation.
source: In contrast, the generation of free SNAP was not detected from ligand-free and ligand-bound SNAP-LC3 during starvation (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Ligand-free Halo is susceptible to proteolysis.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that ligand-free Halo is susceptible to proteolysis but, unlike SNAP, Halo becomes resistant to proteolysis after covalently binding to its ligand and persists in lysosomes (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that free Halo is only detected from ligand-bound Halo-LC3B.

claim: Unlike SNAP, Halo becomes resistant to proteolysis after covalently binding to its ligand and persists in lysosomes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that ligand-free Halo is susceptible to proteolysis but, unlike SNAP, Halo becomes resistant to proteolysis after covalently binding to its ligand and persists in lysosomes (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing Halo and SNAP behavior.

claim: Autophagic flux can be quantitatively determined with pulse-chasable Halo-based reporters.
source: Therefore, autophagic flux can be quantitatively determined with pulse-chasable Halo-based reporters.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data demonstrating the properties of Halo-based reporters.

claim: The amount of free HaloTMR generated from HaloTMR-LC3B was detected as early as 0.5 hr of starvation and increased over time.
source: The amount of free HaloTMR generated from HaloTMR-LC3B was detected as early as 0.5 hr of starvation and increased over time (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The ratio of released HaloTMR to total HaloTMR showed a linear increase of free HaloTMR levels.
source: Calculation of the ratio of released HaloTMR to total HaloTMR (HaloTMR-LC3B+HaloTMR) showed a linear increase of free HaloTMR levels that was readily reproducible (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Pulse-labeling ensures that the starting amount of HaloTMR-LC3B is relatively the same for each experimental condition.
source: The advantages of the processing assay are: (1) pulse-labeling ensures that the starting amount of HaloTMR-LC3B is relatively the same for each experimental condition (here, each time point), (2) the amount of free Halo is a positive readout (i.e. a signal is produced rather than reduced by autophagy), and (3) quantifying the amount of free HaloTMR produced is self-contained without the need for additional controls such as a lysosomal inhibitor control or a loading control.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the pulse-labeling approach.

claim: The amount of free Halo is a positive readout where a signal is produced rather than reduced by autophagy.
source: The advantages of the processing assay are: (1) pulse-labeling ensures that the starting amount of HaloTMR-LC3B is relatively the same for each experimental condition (here, each time point), (2) the amount of free Halo is a positive readout (i.e. a signal is produced rather than reduced by autophagy), and (3) quantifying the amount of free HaloTMR produced is self-contained without the need for additional controls such as a lysosomal inhibitor control or a loading control.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the assay design.

claim: Quantifying the amount of free HaloTMR produced is self-contained without the need for additional controls such as a lysosomal inhibitor control or a loading control.
source: The advantages of the processing assay are: (1) pulse-labeling ensures that the starting amount of HaloTMR-LC3B is relatively the same for each experimental condition (here, each time point), (2) the amount of free Halo is a positive readout (i.e. a signal is produced rather than reduced by autophagy), and (3) quantifying the amount of free HaloTMR produced is self-contained without the need for additional controls such as a lysosomal inhibitor control or a loading control.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the assay design.

claim: The Halo-LC3B processing assay is a simple and sensitive method with a wide linear range to quantitatively monitor autophagic flux in mammalian cells.
source: The Halo-LC3B processing assay is thus a simple and sensitive method with a wide linear range to quantitatively monitor autophagic flux in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data demonstrating the assay's properties.

claim: The number of mGFP-LC3B puncta increased during the first 2 hr of starvation but did not increase thereafter.
source: The number of mGFP-LC3B puncta increased during the first 2 hr of starvation but did not increase thereafter (Figure 2a and c), which is likely due to the quenching of mGFP signal in autolysosomes (Kimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2a and c, with inference about the cause supported by a citation.

claim: The lack of increase in mGFP-LC3B puncta after 2 hr of starvation is likely due to the quenching of mGFP signal in autolysosomes.
source: The number of mGFP-LC3B puncta increased during the first 2 hr of starvation but did not increase thereafter (Figure 2a and c), which is likely due to the quenching of mGFP signal in autolysosomes (Kimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Under growing conditions, many mRFP-LC3B puncta were already present and their high rate of colocalization with LysoTracker revealed them to be lysosomes.
source: Under growing conditions, many mRFP-LC3B puncta were already present and their high rate of colocalization with LysoTracker revealed them to be lysosomes (Figure 2a), demonstrating mRFP's stability in acidic compartments (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2a and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The pre-existing mRFP-LC3B puncta demonstrate mRFP's stability in acidic compartments.
source: Under growing conditions, many mRFP-LC3B puncta were already present and their high rate of colocalization with LysoTracker revealed them to be lysosomes (Figure 2a), demonstrating mRFP's stability in acidic compartments (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: An increase in the number of mRFP-LC3B puncta during starvation was not detected.
source: Furthermore, an increase in the number of mRFP-LC3B puncta during starvation was not detected (Figure 2a and c), likely because the formation of mRFP-LC3B-marked autophagosomes was masked by the pre-existing intense lysosomal mRFP signal (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2a and c.

claim: The lack of increase in mRFP-LC3B puncta during starvation is likely because the formation of mRFP-LC3B-marked autophagosomes was masked by the pre-existing intense lysosomal mRFP signal.
source: Furthermore, an increase in the number of mRFP-LC3B puncta during starvation was not detected (Figure 2a and c), likely because the formation of mRFP-LC3B-marked autophagosomes was masked by the pre-existing intense lysosomal mRFP signal (Katayama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Halo-LC3B labeled with SF650 ligand demonstrated only a few faint punctate structures immediately after labeling.
source: Contrastingly, Halo-LC3B that was labeled with ligand conjugated to fluorogenic SaraFluor 650T (SF650) demonstrated only a few faint punctate structures immediately after labeling, and starvation induced a continuous increase in the number of HaloSF650-positive puncta over time (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2b and c.

claim: Starvation induced a continuous increase in the number of HaloSF650-positive puncta over time.
source: Contrastingly, Halo-LC3B that was labeled with ligand conjugated to fluorogenic SaraFluor 650T (SF650) demonstrated only a few faint punctate structures immediately after labeling, and starvation induced a continuous increase in the number of HaloSF650-positive puncta over time (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2b and c.

claim: Many of the HaloSF650-positive puncta are autolysosomes as they colocalized with LysoTracker and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1.
source: Many of the HaloSF650-positive puncta are autolysosomes as they colocalized with LysoTracker (Figure 2b) and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), which shows that HaloSF650 is stable in acidic lysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from colocalization data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: HaloSF650 is stable in acidic lysosomes.
source: Many of the HaloSF650-positive puncta are autolysosomes as they colocalized with LysoTracker (Figure 2b) and the lysosomal membrane protein LAMP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), which shows that HaloSF650 is stable in acidic lysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data.

claim: Autophagosomes cannot be distinguished from autolysosomes with Halo-LC3 alone.
source: Although autophagosomes cannot be distinguished from autolysosomes with Halo-LC3, the number of ligand-bound Halo puncta formed following pulse-labeling of Halo-based reporters can indicate autophagic flux.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations and capabilities of the Halo-LC3 reporter.

claim: The number of ligand-bound Halo puncta formed following pulse-labeling of Halo-based reporters can indicate autophagic flux.
source: Although autophagosomes cannot be distinguished from autolysosomes with Halo-LC3, the number of ligand-bound Halo puncta formed following pulse-labeling of Halo-based reporters can indicate autophagic flux.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The constitutive accumulation of mRFP in lysosomes often hinders the detection of newly generated autolysosomes with mRFP-mGFP-LC3B.
source: This reporter was originally developed to distinguish between mRFP-positive mGFP-positive (mRFP+mGFP+) autophagosomes and mRFP-positive mGFP-negative (mRFP+mGFP–) autolysosomes, but the constitutive accumulation of mRFP in lysosomes often hinders the detection of newly generated autolysosomes (mRFP+mGFP–) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: HaloSF650-mGFP-LC3 was mostly cytosolic immediately after labeling.
source: In contrast, HaloSF650-mGFP-LC3 was mostly cytosolic immediately after labeling (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Starvation induced the formation of HaloSF650+mGFP+ puncta that represent autophagosomes and HaloSF650+mGFP– puncta that represent autolysosomes.
source: Starvation induced the formation of HaloSF650+mGFP+ puncta that represent autophagosomes (arrowheads) and HaloSF650+mGFP– puncta that represent autolysosomes (arrows) as confirmed by their colocalization with LysoTracker or LAMP1-mRuby3 (Figure 2e and f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2e and f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Adding bafilomycin A1 resulted in the accumulation of HaloSF650+ and mGFP+ in autophagosomes and autolysosomes.
source: Adding the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 resulted in the accumulation of HaloSF650+ and mGFP+ in autophagosomes and autolysosomes (Figure 2e and f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2e and f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The lack of pre-existing lysosomal accumulation makes Halo-mGFP-LC3B a preferable alternative to mRFP-mGFP-LC3B as a fluorescence microscopy-based autophagic flux reporter.
source: Hence, the lack of pre-existing lysosomal accumulation makes Halo-mGFP-LC3B a preferable alternative to mRFP-mGFP-LC3B as a fluorescence microscopy-based autophagic flux reporter.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the comparative experimental data.

claim: Halo-mGFP-LC3B-mRFP can be used in the processing assay, the autophagosome/autolysosome formation assay, and the GFP:RFP ratiometry assay.
source: Adding Halo at the N-terminus of mGFP-LC3B-mRFP yielded a reporter that can be used in the processing assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), the autophagosome/autolysosome formation assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f), and the GFP:RFP ratiometry assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, f, and g.

claim: Halo-mGFP-LC3B-mRFP can be used as a stably expressed 'three-in-one' reporter.
source: Thus, Halo-mGFP-LC3B-mRFP can be used as a stably expressed 'three-in-one' reporter.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing its multiple applications.

claim: Pulse-chasable Halo-based reporters are suitable for monitoring autophagic flux by fluorescence microscopy in addition to the processing assay readout.
source: In summary, pulse-chasable Halo-based reporters are suitable for monitoring autophagic flux by fluorescence microscopy in addition to the processing assay readout.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the section.

claim: A major advantage of the yeast GFP-Atg8 processing assay is its versatility: Atg8 can be replaced with a protein of interest to monitor the activity of selective autophagy.
source: A major advantage of the yeast GFP-Atg8 processing assay is its versatility: Atg8 can be replaced with a protein of interest to monitor the activity of selective autophagy, such as endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-phagy and mitophagy.
evidence: This statement describes an established advantage of the yeast assay.

claim: Halo-mGFP-KDEL localizes to the ER lumen.
source: Hence, we prepared Halo-mGFP-KDEL that localizes to the ER lumen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) and pSu9-Halo-mGFP that localizes to the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: pSu9-Halo-mGFP localizes to the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Hence, we prepared Halo-mGFP-KDEL that localizes to the ER lumen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) and pSu9-Halo-mGFP that localizes to the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Generation of the 33 kDa HaloTMR band from pulse-labeled HaloTMR-mGFP-KDEL was detected in a FIP200-dependent manner upon starvation.
source: Generation of the 33 kDa HaloTMR band from pulse-labeled HaloTMR-mGFP-KDEL was detected in a FIP200-dependent manner upon starvation (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3a and b.

claim: Production of free HaloTMR was a clearer indicator of ER-phagy than the reduction in ER protein levels.
source: Production of free HaloTMR was a clear indicator of ER-phagy than the reduction in ER protein levels (Figure 3a–b vs. Figure 3c-d).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on experimental data in Figures 3a-d.

claim: ER-phagy flux was detected by the formation of HaloSF650+mGFP– puncta that colocalized with LysoTracker and LAMP1.
source: With fluorescence microscopy, ER-phagy flux was detected by the formation of HaloSF650+mGFP– puncta that colocalized with LysoTracker (Figure 3e and f) and LAMP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3e and f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Parkin-mediated mitophagic activity induced by oligomycin and antimycin treatment was detected by pSu9-Halo-mGFP processing.
source: Similarly, Parkin-mediated mitophagic activity induced by oligomycin and antimycin treatment was detected by pSu9-Halo-mGFP processing (Figure 3g and h) as well as the formation of HaloSF650+mGFP– puncta colocalized with the lysosome (Figure 3i and j, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3g and h.

claim: Parkin-mediated mitophagic activity was detected by the formation of HaloSF650+mGFP– puncta colocalized with the lysosome.
source: Similarly, Parkin-mediated mitophagic activity induced by oligomycin and antimycin treatment was detected by pSu9-Halo-mGFP processing (Figure 3g and h) as well as the formation of HaloSF650+mGFP– puncta colocalized with the lysosome (Figure 3i and j, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3i and j and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: An additional 37 kDa HaloTag band was observed in the SDS-PAGE results, which is most likely a cleavage product of the HaloTag constructs.
source: An additional 37 kDa HaloTag band was observed in the SDS-PAGE based results (Figure 3a and g) that is most likely a cleavage product of the HaloTag constructs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed band in Figures 3a and g.

claim: The lack of cytosolic Halo and GFP signal indicates that the 37 kDa cleavage product localizes to the targeted organelle.
source: The lack of cytosolic Halo and GFP signal (Figure 3e and i) indicates that this still-fluorescent product (in-gel fluorescence images in Figure 3a and g) localizes to the targeted organelle and would not result in background signal that might interfere with result interpretation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figures 3e and i.

claim: The Halo-based assays can be adapted to monitor selective autophagic flux.
source: Therefore, the Halo-based assays can be adapted to monitor selective autophagic flux.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with ER-phagy and mitophagy reporters.

claim: Bulk nonselective autophagic flux more accurately reflects total autophagic flux compared to LC3-based methods since LC3 and GABARAP family proteins are preferentially degraded by autophagy.
source: Finally, we examined whether the Halo-based processing assay could be used to detect bulk nonselective autophagic flux, which more accurately reflects total autophagic flux compared to LC3-based methods since LC3 and GABARAP family proteins are preferentially degraded by autophagy (Klionsky et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: LC3 and GABARAP family proteins are preferentially degraded by autophagy.
source: Finally, we examined whether the Halo-based processing assay could be used to detect bulk nonselective autophagic flux, which more accurately reflects total autophagic flux compared to LC3-based methods since LC3 and GABARAP family proteins are preferentially degraded by autophagy (Klionsky et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Halo-mGFP should be taken up randomly into autophagosomes or lysosomes like the yeast Pgk1-GFP reporter.
source: To monitor nonselective clearance of cytosolic material, we constructed Halo-mGFP, which should be taken up randomly into autophagosomes or lysosomes like the yeast Pgk1-GFP reporter (Welter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to the yeast reporter, supported by a citation.

claim: The generation of free HaloTMR from pulse-labeled HaloTMR-mGFP was detected despite occurring at much lower levels than LC3-dependent autophagic flux.
source: Despite occurring at much lower levels than LC3-dependent autophagic flux detected by HaloTMR-LC3B, the lack of lysosomal background allowed us to detect the generation of free HaloTMR from pulse-labeled HaloTMR-mGFP (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4a.

claim: Starvation-induced bulk nonselective autophagic flux was tracked over time by HaloTMR-mGFP processing.
source: Accordingly, we were able to track the progression of starvation-induced bulk nonselective autophagic flux over time by HaloTMR-mGFP processing (Figure 4b and c) and by visualizing the gradual accumulation of HaloSF650 signal in the lysosomes of cells stably expressing Halo-mGFP labeled with SF650 ligand (Figure 4d and e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4b and c.

claim: Starvation-induced bulk nonselective autophagic flux was tracked by visualizing the gradual accumulation of HaloSF650 signal in the lysosomes.
source: Accordingly, we were able to track the progression of starvation-induced bulk nonselective autophagic flux over time by HaloTMR-mGFP processing (Figure 4b and c) and by visualizing the gradual accumulation of HaloSF650 signal in the lysosomes of cells stably expressing Halo-mGFP labeled with SF650 ligand (Figure 4d and e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4d and e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: HaloTMR-mGFP processing and HaloSF650 puncta formation were not observed in FIP200 KO cells.
source: HaloTMR-mGFP processing and HaloSF650 puncta formation were not observed in FIP200 KO cells (Figure 4a and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4a and d.

claim: HaloTMR-mGFP processing was slightly detected in ATG3 KO and ATG5 KO cells.
source: In contrast, HaloTMR-mGFP processing was slightly detected in ATG3 KO and ATG5 KO cells (Figure 4a), which is consistent with our previous finding that the ATG conjugation systems are not completely essential in mammalian cells (Tsuboyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4a and a citation to prior work.

claim: The ATG conjugation systems are not completely essential in mammalian cells.
source: In contrast, HaloTMR-mGFP processing was slightly detected in ATG3 KO and ATG5 KO cells (Figure 4a), which is consistent with our previous finding that the ATG conjugation systems are not completely essential in mammalian cells (Tsuboyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The Halo-GFP processing assay can be used to monitor bulk nonselective autophagic flux, even in cells lacking ATG conjugation system components.
source: These results show that the Halo-GFP processing assay can be used to monitor bulk nonselective autophagic flux, even in cells lacking ATG conjugation system components.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with ATG3 KO and ATG5 KO cells.

claim: The most significant advantage the HaloTag reporters have over currently available ATG8-based reporters and autophagy assays is that they can be used in a pulse-chase manner.
source: The most significant advantage the HaloTag reporters have over currently available ATG8-based reporters and autophagy assays is that they can be used in a pulse-chase manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and comparison with existing methods.

claim: Pulse-chase labeling allows for minimal background noise since unlabeled reporters will not accumulate within lysosomes.
source: This allows for minimal background noise since unlabeled reporters will not accumulate within lysosomes, and for the readout of free Halo to be unambiguously autophagy-dependent since it occurs only when the reporter has been labeled, delivered into, and processed in lysosomes.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the pulse-chase approach.

claim: The readout of free Halo is unambiguously autophagy-dependent since it occurs only when the reporter has been labeled, delivered into, and processed in lysosomes.
source: This allows for minimal background noise since unlabeled reporters will not accumulate within lysosomes, and for the readout of free Halo to be unambiguously autophagy-dependent since it occurs only when the reporter has been labeled, delivered into, and processed in lysosomes.
evidence: This is an inference about the specificity of the assay.

claim: Another major advantage is the dispensation of a lysosome inhibitor control that may affect transcription/translation.
source: Another major advantage is the dispensation of a lysosome inhibitor control that may affect transcription/translation.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of not requiring lysosomal inhibitors.

claim: Reporter processing can be detected by immunoblotting, which is a widely available and commonly used laboratory technique.
source: Furthermore, reporter processing can be detected by immunoblotting, which is a widely available and commonly used laboratory technique.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about laboratory techniques.

claim: Reporter processing can be detected by in-gel imaging if available, which would reduce the time required to obtain results.
source: It can also be detected by in-gel imaging if available, which would reduce the time required to obtain results.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of in-gel imaging.

claim: By replacing the partner protein of Halo, users can easily adapt the assay to monitor their autophagy pathway of interest or the autophagic clearance of a protein of interest.
source: Last, by replacing the partner protein of Halo, users can easily adapt the assay to monitor their autophagy pathway of interest or the autophagic clearance of a protein of interest.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated versatility of the assay.

claim: One limitation of the assay is the need for exogenous expression.
source: One that is inevitable is the need for exogenous expression.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the method.

claim: For experiments that are sensitive to variation in expression levels, clonal isolation may be required.
source: For experiments that are sensitive to variation in expression levels, clonal isolation may be required.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential requirements for certain applications.

claim: The cost of Halo ligands might be prohibitive.
source: Furthermore, the cost of Halo ligands might be prohibitive.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential limitation.

claim: Non-fluorescent Halo ligands, such as 7-bromoheptanol, could be a more cost-effective alternative.
source: A more cost-effective alternative could be the non-fluorescent Halo ligands, such as 7-bromoheptanol, which were developed as blocking agents (Merrill et al., 2019), and Halo band detection would be achieved only by immunoblotting.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Another limitation is the difficulty in quantifying the absolute rate of reporter incorporation into lysosomes precisely due to the gradual degradation of even Haloligand.
source: Another limitation is the difficulty in quantifying the absolute rate of reporter incorporation into lysosomes precisely due to the gradual degradation of even Haloligand.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of the method.

claim: The need to electrophoretically separate the full-length reporter from the free Haloligand band limits the use of this assay for large-scale screening.
source: Additionally, the need to electrophoretically separate the full-length reporter from the free Haloligand band limits the use of this assay for large-scale screening.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of the method.

claim: The good signal-to-noise ratio of Halo reporters in fluorescent imaging makes them ideal reporters for microscopy-based high-content screening.
source: However, the good signal-to-noise ratio of Halo reporters in fluorescent imaging makes them ideal reporters for microscopy-based high-content screening in the same manner as was achieved with GFP-LC3 (Orvedahl et al., 2011; McKnight et al., 2012; Koepke et al., 2020) and dual-fluorescent Rosella-LC3 (Arias-Fuenzalida et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior literature demonstrating similar applications.

claim: Halo-LC3 reporter processing is not suitable for monitoring the activity of non-canonical forms of autophagy, where LC3 is conjugated to single-membrane organelles.
source: Finally, Halo-LC3 reporter processing is not suitable for monitoring the activity of non-canonical forms of autophagy, where LC3 is conjugated to single-membrane organelles (e.g. LC3-associated phagocytosis; Heckmann and Green, 2019; Herb et al., 2020) as the reporter will not be delivered into lysosomes.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of the method, supported by citations.

claim: The Halo-based processing assay is anticipated to be useful to most studies on mammalian autophagy and lysosome-dependent protein clearance.
source: We anticipate the Halo-based processing assay to be useful to most studies on mammalian autophagy and lysosome-dependent protein clearance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of the method.

claim: With Halo-GFP, researchers can investigate the contribution of autophagy proteins by examining whether altering a protein by depletion/inhibition/mutation will affect nonselective autophagic flux.
source: With Halo-GFP, researchers can investigate the contribution of autophagy proteins by examining whether altering a protein by depletion/inhibition/mutation will affect nonselective autophagic flux.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the method.

claim: The Halo-GFP assay may be especially useful to researchers investigating proteins that are directly required for commonly used autophagic flux assays, such as factors involved in the LC3 or GABARAP conjugation systems.
source: This may be especially useful to researchers investigating proteins that are directly required for commonly used autophagic flux assays, such as factors involved in the LC3 or GABARAP conjugation systems.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the method.

claim: Low levels of autophagic flux were detected in ATG3 KO and ATG5 KO cells, which cannot be detected by conventional LC3-based assays.
source: Indeed, we managed to detect low levels of autophagic flux in ATG3 KO and ATG5 KO cells (Figure 4a), which cannot be detected by conventional LC3-based assays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4a and inference about the limitations of LC3-based assays.

claim: Although severely reduced, autophagic flux is not completely blocked in cells lacking the ATG conjugation systems.
source: This result is consistent with the recent consensus that, although severely reduced, autophagic flux is not completely blocked in cells lacking the ATG conjugation systems (reviewed in Mizushima, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Halo-GFP could be potentially used to study microautophagy.
source: Halo-GFP could also be potentially used to study microautophagy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Halo-based reporters have been successfully employed in animal models such as mice and zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, Halo-based reporters have been successfully employed in animal models (England et al., 2015) such as mice (Masch et al., 2018; Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020) and zebrafish (Wan et al., 2019), which suggest that the processing assay could be an additional method for assessing in vivo autophagic flux, e.g. when comparing autophagic flux among tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The processing assay could be an additional method for assessing in vivo autophagic flux, e.g. when comparing autophagic flux among tissues.
source: Furthermore, Halo-based reporters have been successfully employed in animal models (England et al., 2015) such as mice (Masch et al., 2018; Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020) and zebrafish (Wan et al., 2019), which suggest that the processing assay could be an additional method for assessing in vivo autophagic flux, e.g. when comparing autophagic flux among tissues.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by citations showing Halo use in animal models.

claim: The Halo-based processing assay can be used to monitor mammalian autophagic flux quantitatively and reliably with relative ease.
source: In conclusion, the Halo-based processing assay can be used to monitor mammalian autophagic flux quantitatively and reliably with relative ease.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Halo-based reporters can be readily observed by fluorescence microscopy.
source: The Halo-based reporters can also be readily observed by fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing fluorescence microscopy applications.

claim: Besides serving as an alternative to conventional autophagic flux assays, the Halo-based assay has a myriad of potential applications that may lead to the discovery of new aspects and thus a deeper understanding of mammalian autophagy.
source: Besides serving as an alternative to conventional autophagic flux assays, the Halo-based assay has a myriad of potential applications that may lead to the discovery of new aspects and thus a deeper understanding of mammalian autophagy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the method.

claim: While this manuscript was being prepared, an independent study on the use of Halo-based reporters to monitor autophagic flux was published.
source: While this manuscript was being prepared, an independent study on the use of Halo-based reporters to monitor autophagic flux was published (Rudinskiy et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to concurrent work.

claim: Rudinskiy et al. sought to overcome the issue of lysosomal RFP accumulation with Halo-based reporters that can be fluorescently 'activated' upon binding to fluorescent ligands.
source: In contrast to our main aim of developing a reporter processing assay for mammalian cells, Rudinskiy et al. sought to overcome the issue of lysosomal RFP accumulation with Halo-based reporters that can be fluorescently 'activated' upon binding to fluorescent ligands.
evidence: This statement describes the approach of a concurrent study, supported by a citation.

claim: The 'activation' of Halo-based reporters is achieved not only by the introduction of fluorescent Halo ligand but also by the stabilization of Halo against proteolysis after ligand binding.
source: Our study demonstrated that the 'activation' of Halo-based reporters is achieved not only by the introduction of fluorescent Halo ligand but, importantly, also by the stabilization of Halo against proteolysis after ligand binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Ligand binding is known to increase a protein's thermal stability.
source: Since ligand binding is known to increase a protein's thermal stability (Celej et al., 2003; Vedadi et al., 2006) and proteolytic resistance (Stankunas et al., 2003; Park and Marqusee, 2005; Kaur et al., 2018), we selected two protein tags that covalently bind with their respective ligands as candidate tags: Halo (Los et al., 2008) and SNAP-tag (SNAP) (Keppler et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ligand binding is known to increase a protein's proteolytic resistance.
source: Since ligand binding is known to increase a protein's thermal stability (Celej et al., 2003; Vedadi et al., 2006) and proteolytic resistance (Stankunas et al., 2003; Park and Marqusee, 2005; Kaur et al., 2018), we selected two protein tags that covalently bind with their respective ligands as candidate tags: Halo (Los et al., 2008) and SNAP-tag (SNAP) (Keppler et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.
